e: Introduction

For Grandpa Jack — father, grandfather, World War II veteran, college basketball star, PhD, teacher, coach, and my mentor. The man I wanted to become. A leader who was never loud. A teacher who never lectured. Always a coach, never a critic. He had a gift for getting the best out of people. He knew how to say “You’ve come a long way” and “Job well done” while letting me know, “You’re not quite done; the best has yet to come.” Love you, Gramps.
Introduction

American history can be read as a series of final scores, headlines, and game summaries. Historians have written about the teams, the players, and the coaches, carefully documenting who won, who lost, and by how much. But the meaning of those outcomes has never been settled by the final score. That is where historiography, the history of how history is written, becomes important. It asks questions that a box score cannot answer: What game was being played? What were the rules? What were we playing for? And perhaps most importantly, who kept score?
Introduction

Historians do not approach the past free from the assumptions, questions, and circumstances of their own time. Each generation brings different perspectives to the historical record, asking new questions and sometimes reaching very different conclusions about the same events. Every account of American history keeps its own score, and every historian serves as a different scorekeeper, bringing their own rules, perspectives, and biases to the game. This account is no exception.
Introduction

Historiography is the lifeblood of academic history, yet the general reader may know little of the competing interpretations and ongoing disputes that shape our current understanding. Virtually every major period in the American experience has been the subject of fierce intellectual combat: the motives behind European colonization, the consequences of westward expansion, the origins of the Civil War, the meaning of Reconstruction, the rise of industrial capitalism, and the struggle for civil rights. Few subjects, however, illustrate the persistence of historical disagreement better than the American Revolution. Almost as soon as the Republic came into existence, Americans began arguing over what had brought it about, who deserved credit for its success, and what it was supposed to accomplish. Those questions have never entirely disappeared.
Introduction

What follows is an examination of the principal ways historians have interpreted the American past, the arguments that have shaped those interpretations, and the ways in which each generation has reconsidered the history of the nation.
Introduction

For more than a century after independence, American historians largely agreed on what the story meant. David Ramsay wrote the Revolution as a triumph of liberty over tyranny, and George Bancroft carried that triumph across ten volumes, adding the hand of Providence. In 1913 Charles Beard broke the agreement. His Economic Interpretation of the Constitution argued that the framers had acted on their own economic interests, and for a generation the Progressive historians read American history as a contest between the propertied and everyone else. After the Second World War, Daniel Boorstin and other consensus historians pushed back, arguing instead that the ideas, values, and experiences Americans shared mattered more than the divisions and conflicts between them. The debate between these interpretations centered on questions of motive, class, and the forces that shaped American society. Despite their differences, both schools of thought shared an antiquated axiom: the story belonged to the powerful.
Introduction

Beginning in the 1960s, historians challenged that assumption. A generation of social historians turned to the people the older narratives had left at the edges: women, workers, the enslaved, and Native nations. Eugene Genovese’s Roll, Jordan, Roll recovered the world enslaved people made for themselves within slavery’s limits. In the West, Patricia Nelson Limerick’s The Legacy of Conquest replaced Turner’s frontier with a continuous history of conquest, and Richard White’s The Middle Ground showed Native peoples and Europeans negotiating a shared world in which neither side could simply dictate terms. More recently, Ned Blackhawk has argued that American history cannot be understood at all without Native peoples at its center. The historical narrative did more than add new teams and expand its rosters. It began to ask different questions. Historians came to see that an outcome means little on its own; it has to be set in context, explained by its causes, and followed forward through what continued and what changed. A final score, in other words, says nothing about how the game was played.
Introduction

But the inclusive narrative carried with it a new set of challenges, beyond simply merging the old with the new. How do historians include not only the existence of those long excluded, but their merits, their accomplishments, and their influence, without diminishment or dismissal? And how do they do it without rewriting the record, or the rulebook, as an act of retribution: vacating wins and taking down championship banners?
Introduction

It is a difficult job, made harder by the historian’s own purpose and bias, and the attempts have tended toward three extremes. The first gave the new actors a place in the story the way the Washington Generals took the court against the Harlem Globetrotters. They had the privilege of competing against the best, occupying the same court, but solely because the game requires two teams to play. Real opponents, predestined to lose, who proved ineffectual against the inevitable. Those accounts acknowledged that Native nations, the enslaved, and women had been present, but they kept the older Euro-American narrative and the heroes of Manifest Destiny at center stage.
Introduction

The second cast them as victims. They entered the story the way Robert Griffin III is often remembered: not as the 2012 Offensive Rookie of the Year who seemed ready to remake the quarterback position, but as a knee buckling on a January afternoon against Seattle, while the coaches who should have pulled him watched from the sideline. Here the systems themselves (racism, sexism, discrimination, exploitation) took the center of the story, and the people living under them became an injury report, evidence of what had been done to them. Systems and institutions did shape the experiences and opportunities of those long relegated to the margins of American history, but a history told only through them leaves little room for the people.
Introduction

The third runs in the opposite direction, pivoting from the injury report to the highlight reel. Writing history from the bottom up, these historians searched for the ways ordinary people resisted, negotiated, carved out spaces of their own, and shaped American culture and politics. At its best, the approach restored people to the story. At its extreme, it turns them into the hero of an underdog movie. The Blind Side told Michael Oher’s rise from poverty to the NFL as a story of grit rewarded and a family’s generosity. In 2023, after Oher alleged that the arrangement he had lived under had been misrepresented to him as an adoption, a claim the Tuohys disputed, a Tennessee judge ended the conservatorship that had governed his affairs. The heartwarming version had left the hardest questions outside the frame: who controlled his story, and who profited from it. Romanticized history makes the same mistake. It turns every life into a triumph and, in doing so, understates how restrictive, violent, and crushing the systems around those lives actually were.
Introduction

None of the three mirrors the full record. Rather than focusing solely on victors and victims, the best history examines the relationships among power, opportunity, resistance, and individual agency. It asks who made the decisions, whose interests those decisions served, how ordinary people responded to forces beyond their control, and how those responses shaped both immediate outcomes and the course of later events. It recognizes the importance of individuals as well as institutions, considers societies alongside the systems that shaped them, and refuses to reduce the people who lived within those structures to mere beneficiaries or casualties of historical change. Complexity and nuance often obscure the patterns we find most obvious and complicate the endings that make us comfortable. But they do not erase them; nor do they absolve historical actors of responsibility for their choices and actions. Knowing more about our past does not require us to abandon judgment. It asks us to make that judgment with greater care, a fuller understanding of circumstances, and a clearer appreciation of the choices people made and the consequences they produced.
Introduction

The people who survived conquest and slavery, those who persevered through exclusion and discrimination were, as I have argued in my own research, neither powerless, nor passive subjects, but autonomous agents who actively engaged with the world. The historian’s responsibility is to account for both realities: the forces that constrained an individual’s life and the agency that individual exercised within them.
Introduction

That is why the book carries two questions in its title, and why they return throughout its chapters: Who belonged? Who decided? Each chapter examines those questions in its own time and place: who was considered part of the community, who was not, and who possessed the power to make those distinctions?
How to read this book
Every chapter includes four tools.
How to read this book

The first tool is a set of three questions to ask of any conflict: What does the law say? What do the morals mandate? Who holds the power? When the Fugitive Slave Law passed in 1850, Daniel Webster stood by the law, Henry David Thoreau stood on conscience, and in 1854 William Lloyd Garrison literally set the law on fire, when he burned a replica of the Constitution itself.
How to read this book

The second tool makes a clear distinction: explaining is not excusing. Cultural legacies are real, they are observable patterns of the past. They are not mandates for behavior, nor are they predestined pathways into the future; we all have free will. When this book traces a sequence of similar behaviors, either by individuals or institutions, which span across generations, it is provided solely to explain the past, not to excuse it.
How to read this book

Footnotes are the third tool. Most textbooks hide their doubts; this one puts them at the bottom of the page. The notes tell you how strong the evidence is behind each claim: which numbers are counts and which are estimates, which famous lines were said and which were invented later. “Fifty-four forty or fight!” has echoed through textbooks as a slogan of Polk’s 1844 campaign; the notes show you the evidence that it wasn’t.
How to read this book

The fourth tool is a question: so what? If a student can identify why history matters, they can transform that knowledge into a material gain or a real, actionable benefit. Each chapter concludes with a contemporary parallel, inviting you to consider where those connections hold, where they break down, and what they reveal about the society we have inherited. The purpose is not to suggest that history repeats itself or that the present can be understood simply by looking backward. It is to give you the opportunity to examine those connections for yourself, question the comparisons, and decide whether or not the past can provide sensible answers for today and solutions for our future.
Acknowledgments

Thank you to all of my former students and athletes: every kid in my classroom or in my hallway, either with me on the field or on the bench beside me. You believed in me, and I always wanted nothing but the best for you. I think I learned more from you than you ever did from me. Among my life’s greatest privileges were the opportunities to be your teacher, your coach, and your friend. Thank you for all of the love and support you’ve shown me over the years, and above all, thank you for helping me become the man I am today.
Introduction
“Ancora imparo.” I am still learning.
Introduction

Most history textbooks tell the story of human existence by arranging a few notable events into an insipid chronology of names and dates. Students regularly learn what happened, who was involved, where and when it took place. But rarely do they understand why it happened, whose interests shaped the outcome, or how historians arrived at their conclusions. That first question matters most: without the why, history becomes a record of the past rather than a way to understand it.
Introduction

Even the way textbooks are organized reinforces the problem. Bolded terms, sidebar definitions, chapter summaries, and multiple-choice review questions help students remember what is likely to appear on a standardized test, but they also teach students to treat history as a closed case file: find the term, memorize the definition, select the correct answer, and move on. That is not how historians work. Historians begin with questions, not answers. They weigh evidence, compare competing accounts, argue about motives, and revise their conclusions when the evidence demands it. Students deserve the same experience: evidence that does not always point in the same direction, and the discovery that understanding the past requires judgment, not simply recall.
Introduction

Understanding the causes, reasoning, and justifications behind human behavior unlocks our innate curiosity and our desire to explore the unknown. Children know this instinctively, which is why they see learning as fun. Somewhere along the way, history turns into something we absorb rather than something we explore. True crime proves the instinct never left us.
Introduction

When confronted with a horrific crime, we struggle to reconcile the act with the person who committed it. How could someone who looks like us, lives next door, or works beside us cross a line we regard as unthinkable?
Introduction

True crime works like a psychological autopsy. Its audience combs through a killer’s childhood, relationships, and breaking points, trying to reverse-engineer how an ordinary person becomes a monster. Historians perform the same autopsy on the past. How did ordinary people come to own other people, drive their neighbors off ancestral land, or march off to kill their own countrymen? The answer rarely turns out to be monsters. More often, it turns out to be people much like us. Understanding is not justifying.
Introduction

The resemblance ends at the verdict. True crime almost always delivers a clean moral arc: a transgression, a hunt, an unmasking, a resolution. History rarely offers that comfort. Justice is often delivered too little, too late, or not at all, and the guilty frequently die in their own beds instead of on a prisoner’s cot. That leaves the historian with the why, and the why leads to the questions that still matter today.
Introduction

True crime offers the most dramatic hunt for the why, but the most common form of historical analysis happens every day in break rooms, barbershops, social media posts, or wherever people argue about last night’s game. History, like sports, often comes with a list of winners and losers, defined solely by the outcomes they produced. But an outcome is only the final score, and anyone who watches sports knows the scoreboard does not tell the whole story. That is why I often use sports as a metaphor for history: knowing who won the Super Bowl is neither as truthful nor as useful as understanding how or why they won.
Introduction

When sports fans debate the greatest of all time, compare players across eras, or try to explain a team’s collapse, they are doing more than arguing over statistics. They are practicing the historian’s craft in a form most people already understand, on a gridiron instead of an empire. Sports leave behind a record of performance, decisions, changing conditions, and consequences. The challenge is to sort through that record, separate the causes from the circumstances, and explain why one player, team, or era turned out differently from another.
Introduction

None of those arguments runs hotter than the debate over the greatest of all time, and none better exposes a habit historians call presentism: judging the past through the lens of the present. Many of the fans who argue loudest about Michael Jordan never saw him play. They know him through highlight reels, box scores, and documentaries, and they measure him against a game that now runs faster and shoots far more three-pointers than his ever did. For sports fans, presentism results in endless and harmless arguments over hypotheticals. Applied to history, it is far more consequential, because it skews our understanding of both past and present.
Introduction

Textbooks also leave out the reader’s freedom to remain uncertain or unconvinced. History is full of moments when the outcome was anything but certain. People made decisions in the moment, not knowing whether they would succeed, or even survive. We have the luxury of hindsight; they didn’t, and that difference matters. Looking backward, it is easy to arrange events into a logical sequence and mistake the outcome for the inevitable conclusion. Textbooks often present the past as a straight line from one event to the next, as though the people involved were simply carrying out a script whose ending had already been written. But history was not inevitable to those who lived it. Revolutions could fail. Armies could lose. Political coalitions could collapse. Decisions that seem obvious in retrospect were often uncertain, dangerous, and deeply contested at the time. When a textbook removes that uncertainty, it removes the stakes. The reader knows what happened but never feels what it meant to face the possibility that everything might turn out differently.
Introduction

Sportscasters often say a game was closer than the score would indicate, and that is the closest thing to real analysis most people ever hear. In other words, scoreboards can be misleading. The final score shows who had the better night, not who has the better team. The National Football League has a saying for this: “on any given Sunday.” A scoreboard does not show whether a team played without its injured superstar, if the head coach got ejected, or that a sudden gust of wind pushed the game-winning field goal wide right.
Introduction

The casual fan may read the headlines, watch the highlights, even listen to the postgame interviews, and still not know how the game was won. The diehard, the stat junkie, can name the last twenty Super Bowls, the final scores, the MVPs, and perhaps even the color of the Gatorade dumped on the head coach. But what the diehard often cannot explain is why those players and teams succeeded where others failed. The diehard and the history buff are two sides of the same coin, and they prove the same point. Stats and records, like names and dates, can help win a game of Trivial Pursuit or impress guests at a dinner party; they cannot explain why the game, or the past, turned out the way it did, or, more importantly, why it matters today. Even the diehard is a fan in the front row: the seat is great, but the place to understand the game is up in the booth with the coaches, where the whole field comes into view. That is the difference between surface-level knowledge and deeper understanding, and it is the whole ballgame.
Introduction

In sports, as in history, context matters. Scoreboards, snapshots, and highlight reels often oversimplify, exaggerate, even twist the truth about a player or a team, whereas the game film, known in the coaching world as “the eye in the sky,” does not lie. Some figures benefit from a nostalgic, forgiving record. Jerry West, “the Logo,” remains one of the most respected and revered players of all time, even though he lost eight of the nine NBA Finals he played in. George Washington, the undisputed father of the country, lost more battles than he won, by Mount Vernon’s own account. At Long Island in 1776 he misjudged the British movements and let them trap the Continental Army against the East River, a failure that could have ended the Revolution in its first summer. Washington ordered a silent evacuation across the river by night, and when dawn broke with part of the army still on the Brooklyn shore, a heavy fog settled over the river and covered the last crossings. The scoreboard records a defeat. The game film shows an army that survived to fight again.
Introduction

Others suffer the cruelty of being captured by their worst moments. Bill Buckner collected 2,715 hits and is remembered for a single ground ball through his legs in the 1986 World Series. The scoreboard leaves out that his ankles were so worn down he began treating them five hours before game time, that his manager had replaced him on defense late in every one of the team’s previous postseason wins, and that the Red Sox still had an entire Game 7 to win the series. Leon Lett won three championships with the Dallas Cowboys and made two Pro Bowls, yet he is immortalized for a showboat fumble that turned a Super Bowl highlight into an all-time blooper. Herbert Hoover is remembered as the president who could have prevented the Great Depression but refused to use federal power. In truth, however, Hoover did not sit idly by; he approved the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and signed the Emergency Relief and Construction Act. Both proved too little, too late, and neither appears on the scoreboard. Richard Nixon opened relations with China, established the Environmental Protection Agency, and signed Title IX into law, yet a single word, Watergate, defines him. A narrative can grow so powerful that it distorts historical facts or downplays them.
Introduction

Sports fans may never agree on who is the best, but no serious fan would argue that the Lakers of the 1960s were a bad team or that Jim Kelly was a horrible quarterback. Those Lakers lost six NBA Finals to the Boston Celtics in eight years, and Kelly’s Buffalo Bills lost four straight Super Bowls. Yet history is often told as a simplistic binary of good and evil, of winner and loser, without any room for nuance or context. Consider Christopher Columbus, Thomas Jefferson, Henry Ford, and Robert Oppenheimer. Columbus is either the daring navigator who connected two worlds or the man who opened them to conquest and enslavement. Jefferson wrote that all men are created equal and enslaved more than six hundred people over his lifetime. Ford put the nation on wheels with the moving assembly line and the five-dollar day, and he used his own newspaper to spread antisemitism. Oppenheimer led the scientists who built the atomic bomb, then warned against the weapons that followed it, until the government stripped him of his security clearance. Each belongs on both sides of the ledger, and a scoreboard has room for only one.
Introduction

A ledger can record the history of a whole society, and a society can cook its own books. After the Civil War, white Southerners built a new account of why they had fought. The war, this version claimed, concerned states’ rights, not slavery. The men who led secession had left little room for that interpretation. Mississippi’s declaration of secession stated plainly, “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.” In March 1861, Confederate vice president Alexander Stephens called slavery the cornerstone of the new government and declared that Black people could never stand as the equals of white people. The Lost Cause rewrote that record anyway, and its defenders organized to make the new version stick.
Introduction

The United Daughters of the Confederacy, founded in 1894, helped carry the story into public memory. The organization raised monuments, influenced school curricula, and policed textbooks. In 1919, its former historian-general, Mildred Rutherford, wrote a textbook guide that condemned books identifying slavery as the cause of the war. The monuments rose in two major waves: the first between 1900 and the 1920s, as segregation took hold across the South; the second from the mid-1950s to the late 1960s, amid the struggle over desegregation and voting rights. Their placement carried a message beyond remembrance. The first wave helped give Jim Crow a heroic past. The second answered the movement challenging its survival.
Introduction

The consequences reached beyond monuments and classrooms. The language of states’ rights became a familiar defense of segregation, while the Lost Cause presented the Confederacy as a noble struggle for constitutional liberty rather than a government founded to preserve slavery. A century after the war, the false account still served a political purpose. The war delivered emancipation. The story told about the war helped defend and legitimize the racial order and institutions that replaced it.
Introduction

Reconstruction suffered a similar fate, and this time historians helped write the wrong story. For the first time, Black men voted, held public office, established schools, and built institutions of their own. William Dunning of Columbia University and his students recast the period as a corrupt failure: ignorant Black officeholders manipulated by scheming carpetbaggers, while vindictive Northerners punished a defeated South. Their interpretation dominated textbooks for decades. W. E. B. Du Bois challenged it in Black Reconstruction (1935), but his account received little attention from the historical establishment for a generation.
Introduction

The Dunning School did more than discredit Reconstruction. It supplied an argument for dismantling its achievements. If Black political participation had produced corruption and misgovernment, the reasoning went, then restricting the Black vote could be presented as a necessary correction. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and white primaries helped accomplish that exclusion. In 2015, historian Eric Foner described the Dunning interpretation as part of the “edifice of the Jim Crow System.” The false history turned the brief experiment in interracial democracy into evidence against democracy itself. It gave Jim Crow a past to blame and a justification to continue.
Introduction

The West was not empty, but the story said it was. In 1845, New York editor John O’Sullivan gave the claim its name: manifest destiny — America’s God-given right to spread across the continent, as if Providence had already assigned the land. Textbooks repeated the phrase until a political argument began to sound like a historical fact. If God had allotted the continent to the United States, then taking Native land could be called settlement, and the nations already living there became obstacles to expansion rather than peoples with claims of their own.
Introduction

The policy followed the logic. In the nineteenth century, the United States used treaties, warfare, and removal to dispossess Native nations. Later, the Dawes Act of 1887 divided tribal lands into individual allotments and opened the remainder to non-Native settlement. Tribal landholdings fell from approximately 138 million acres to 48 million by 1934. The boarding schools pursued the same project of remaking Native life through a different means. Carlisle opened in 1879, and its founder, Richard Henry Pratt, stated the purpose in 1892: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.” Land could be taken from a people; their children could be separated from their families and taught to abandon their languages and cultures. Manifest Destiny did more than explain expansion. It made dispossession sound like a national mission. The story supplied the permission; government policy carried it out.
Introduction

Who gets to write history? For most of the human record the answer is whoever got the final say — the literate, the powerful, the victorious — and overwhelmingly men. Women were there. They were rarely the ones writing it down.
Introduction

Historians work from sources. A primary source comes from someone who was there: a diary, a letter, a newspaper story filed that week, a photograph. But a source by itself is not an answer, because a source has to be placed. Every Star Wars film opens with a block of yellow words crawling up into the dark, telling the audience what has already happened; without them, Darth Vader striding through a captured ship is just noise. Historical context is the opening crawl. So a historian reading a document asks what was going on around it, who wrote it and what he meant to accomplish, what argument he was driving at, what came of it, and whether he can be trusted at all. Columbus, writing to the monarchs who had paid for the voyage, had every reason to describe a paradise worth paying for again. And no single witness settles anything: a fight breaks out at school and thirty students give thirty different accounts, which is why historians collect as many versions as they can find. Out of that work come interpretations, and two historians can read the same record and reach opposite conclusions — two books about the Vietnam War can describe two different wars. As I tell my students, there are three sides to every story: mine, yours, and what actually happened. The truth is often more complicated than we think, or want to believe.
Introduction

How will history remember me? Will it tell my whole story? Will it be accurate? Will it be fair? I often find myself asking those questions when I write about historical figures, and wondering whether I have done them justice. If they could speak to us today, what would they say? What would they want us to know about their lives that has been overlooked, misrepresented, or misunderstood? We cannot give them back their voices, but we can tell their stories with the care and honesty they deserve, mindful that we are speaking for those who can no longer speak for themselves.
Introduction

The first place to put that lesson to work is the story Americans have long told about the continent before European arrival. North America, the story goes, stood as a pristine wilderness: forests untouched, landscapes unaltered by human hands. That image shaped how later generations understood discovery and settlement, while practically erasing any evidence that people already here ever existed. They were not a few scattered bands moving across an empty continent, but millions of people farming, building, trading, and governing. The story took shape in the hands of those who arrived later, and it served their purposes. An empty continent invited discovery; a wilderness justified settlement. Look beyond that familiar account, and a different history comes into view. The Pristine Myth is where we begin.
A different approach

This is a survey of American history from the worlds that existed here before 1492 through the end of the Civil War in 1865, the first half of the two-semester sequence. While it covers the standard first-semester timeline, it approaches that history from angles most textbooks avoid. Rather than simply recounting the familiar sequence of events, it examines the people, competing interests, institutions, and struggles for power that defined the American experience. The chronology remains intact, but the book organizes that timeline around complex questions, controversial interpretations, and the competing arguments that shaped the nation’s development. It is currently free and unpublished, written and revised while it is being taught. The chapters are grouped into units drawn by argument rather than by era, and each unit opens with a guiding question.
A different approach

There is a business side behind the disconnect between students and textbooks. Publishers want to sell their books to school districts across the country, particularly in large markets such as Texas and California. That means producing a book that can satisfy a wide range of expectations without upsetting the people who decide what gets taught. The safest course is often to soften the edges.
A different approach

Two things set this book apart from the conventional commercial survey. First, it advances a single argument that runs through the whole text: the history of America belongs to all the people who helped shape it. Native nations, the enslaved, and ordinary men and women from every background appear as historical actors in their own right, alongside the explorers, founders, political leaders, and generals who usually occupy the center of the story. Their ambitions, choices, and struggles are examined within the circumstances of their time. No one is reduced to a hero or villain; the reader is left to weigh the decisions people made and the consequences that followed.
A different approach

Second, the notes do more than document sources. They examine the evidence itself. They distinguish authentic historical statements from quotations fabricated or misattributed long after the fact, identify where the record is uncertain, and show where scholars disagree. A student can watch how historical knowledge is established, where interpretations diverge, and why some conclusions rest on firmer ground than others. Historical method is not confined to a sidebar or treated as an abstract exercise. It becomes part of the reading, giving students the opportunity to practice the historian’s craft as they move through the text.
A different approach

At first, I offered my own material as a supplement to the standard textbook, and students were free to cite either one. Before long, I noticed several of my students had started citing my work instead. I asked my class for a show of hands: Who preferred my chapters? To my surprise, nearly two-thirds raised their hands. I asked what, specifically, made my chapters land for them. One student said, “The textbook feels like work and I lose interest quickly. I can actually read yours and stay focused.” Another explained that my chapters included anecdotes and context that helped make the material easier to understand. Some appreciated the variety of perspectives, saying they never felt pushed toward any particular conclusion. Years later, when I resumed teaching on a college campus, I noticed the same pattern: by the middle of the semester, most of my college students were citing my work rather than the assigned textbook.
What this book is not

It is not a document reader, a reference encyclopedia, or a substitute for the primary sources students are expected to examine for themselves. It assumes you will bring those sources into the reading and engage them alongside the text. It also makes no attempt to include every term or topic found in a comprehensive survey. The book is written to be read from beginning to end, not consulted. Some material has been adapted from OpenStax under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License and is identified on the Attribution page; the rest is my own.
How a chapter fits a class session

You should not have to rebuild your course to use this book. Twenty chapters carry the survey from the worlds before 1492 to 1865, and a chapter is the pre-class reading for one session. They run six to nine thousand words — twenty to thirty pages — which is one sitting, not one week.
How a chapter fits a class session

Each chapter ends with four to seven Questions for Consideration. They are not review questions, and they have no answer key, because none of them has a single answer. They ask a student to take a position and defend it: which single event made the war inevitable, whether a lawful thing can be immoral, which of three men answered an unjust law correctly. They are written to be the first ten minutes of your class rather than a quiz.
How a chapter fits a class session

My own courses run on three steps: Approach, Analyze, and Demonstrate. The chapter is the Approach—students come to class having already encountered the material, equipped with a method rather than simply a summary. The session is where they Analyze. The assignment is where they Demonstrate.
How a chapter fits a class session

You do not have to adopt any of that to use the book. The only expectation it places on a syllabus is that students read the chapter before they walk in. If you lecture straight through, the chapter does the narrative work and leaves your lecture free to argue with it. Either way, the reading carries the story and the questions carry the argument.
How a chapter fits a class session

Chapters are grouped into units drawn by argument rather than by era. Each unit opens with a short essay posing the question its chapters answer, which gives you a natural place to start a week or a module.
The notes as an assignment engine

The notes are where the uncertainty lives. They record where a claim came from, what had to be corrected, and what could not be confirmed—making them among the most useful teaching materials in the book. Three examples illustrate the point. The Oregon chapter says the cry “Fifty-four forty or fight!” has echoed through textbooks ever since, and the note explains the careful verb: scholarship going back to Edwin Miles in 1957 established that it was never an 1844 campaign slogan but surfaced during the Oregon debate of 1845–46. The Cold Harbor chapter recounts the most famous scene of the battle—soldiers pinning their names to their coats the night before the assault—and then states plainly that it may not have happened. The chapter on emancipation quotes Lincoln’s August 1862 remarks to a Black delegation and notes that the printed account describes itself as “merely given as the substance of the President’s remarks,” not a verbatim record, and that a second printing differs in wording.
The notes as an assignment engine

Each of those moments is an assignment: find a claim this chapter treats as uncertain, state the standard that makes it uncertain, and cite the page. A chatbot might produce a plausible answer, but it cannot reproduce the reasoning in these notes without the text in front of it. Students have to open the book.
The Then and Now question — what it is for

Then and Now, the short block after the Questions for Consideration, does one thing in two moves. First it states a contemporary parallel as a claim, with a note behind it, because a parallel offered as a question commits to nothing and a student can agree with it for free. Then it tells the student to go after the claim. The Reform chapter closes this way: “Test it. Does that pairing hold, or does it reduce four men into two positions? Or set it aside and bring your own: find a cause today where allies agree on the goal and split over the methodology, and say which methodology the record suggests actually changes a country.”
The Then and Now question — what it is for

Both branches are deliberate. A student who takes the first has to argue against the book, which means reading the chapter closely enough to find where the comparison strains. A student who takes the second has to build a parallel that appears nowhere in the chapter, the lecture, or the syllabus, and then defend it with the chapter’s evidence. Neither can be produced from a prompt, because neither has a correct answer sitting somewhere to be retrieved. In my own sections the past-to-present move is what students consistently rate highest, which is why it sits in the spine of the chapter rather than in a sidebar.
The Then and Now question — what it is for

The parallels to the present are not decorative additions or convenient comparisons. They are part of the argument each chapter develops. The Constitution chapter ends by showing how the arithmetic of the Great Compromise continues to shape presidential elections. The Market Revolution closes with the Panic of 1819, a financial crisis whose consequences bear a striking resemblance to those of 2008. The Peculiar Institution ends with two institutions established by the same generation of free Black Americans, one of which remains standing today. A House Divided closes with two universities whose athletic teams still carry the name Rebels, although the word never meant the same thing in both places. The War for the Union ends with Benjamin Butler inventing “contraband of war” to get around the Fugitive Slave Law, and with the legal wall every administration since has had to navigate. These connections are not departures from the history being told. They reveal how its consequences continued to shape the country long after the events themselves had passed.
Three habits, taught rather than described

Three habits run through the book, taught by use rather than explained in a sidebar. They are not evenly distributed, and you should know which is which before you build a syllabus around any of them.
Three habits, taught rather than described

Law, morals, and power, where the material supports it. For Americans, the idea of progress has long been the shared premise; the means of achieving it has been the conflict. The premise appears in successive promises—an errand into the wilderness, a more perfect union, a new birth of freedom, the Social Gospel, the Great Society—and in successive indictments: the jeremiad, “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,” “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?,” a cross of gold, the iron heel of capitalism, a dream deferred. Every one of them, promise or indictment, assumes the nation can become better. The indictments hold the country to its own standard, not against it. What none of them settles is what better looks like, or how to reach it.
Three habits, taught rather than described

When a chapter arrives at that conflict, the book lays out the three instruments a movement can reach for—law, moral argument, and power—and asks which of them actually moved the country. Two chapters are built on this framework and name it: The American Reformation, where it stands as a section of its own, and A House Divided, where the Anthony Burns case forces the question I put to every class: whether something lawful can be immoral. The rest of the book never requires the framework, and it is not imposed where the material does not call for it.
Three habits, taught rather than described

Explaining is not excusing. The Peculiar Institution tests the chapter’s own premise on a population nobody in the chapter is arguing about, then stops. A legacy explains; it does not command. Cultural legacies can account for a stereotype and can become convenient vehicles for justifying present conditions; they are not predestination orders. The Peculiar Institution is where the book tests that principle most directly, with a single cross-reference in The War for the Union. It also serves as the guardrail beneath all twenty Then and Now blocks. Each claims that the past reaches the present; this is the line that keeps those connections from hardening into determinism.
Three habits, taught rather than described

Reading between the sources. Every chapter carries notes—twenty to seventy-one apiece. Four chapters label their corrections in bold throughout: Manifest Destiny, A House Divided, The War for the Union, and A New Birth of Freedom. Those are the Civil War-era chapters in which the sources fought hardest. The remaining chapters do the same corrective work without the label.
